title: Abbasid revolution

text:
The Abbasid revolution (Arabic: اَلثَّوْرَة اَلْعَبَّاسِيَّةِ, romanized: aṯ-Ṯawra al-ʿAbbāsiyyah), was the overthrow of the Umayyad Caliphate (661–750), the second major caliphate, by the Hashimiyya movement, resulting in the establishment of the Abbasid Caliphate (750–1517), the third major caliphate.
The Abbasid revolution originated in the eastern province of Khorasan in the mid-8th century, fuelled by widespread discontent with Umayyad rule. The revolt was led by the Abbasid dynasty, descendants of al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, an uncle of the Islamic prophet Muhammad from the Banu Hashim. Although Abu Muslim, who directed the uprising in Khurāsān, played a decisive organizational and military role, his precise ethnic origins remain debated in the sources. 
The  revolutionary forces (ahl Khurāsān) were heavily composed of long-settled Arab tribal groups in Khurāsān (Khorasani Arabs), many of whom were affiliated with South Arabian (Yamani) confederations that had been established there since the early Islamic conquests. They formed the backbone and majority of the forces and brought the Abbasids to power.Non-Arab Muslim converts (mawālī), including Iranian Muslims, and local supporters participated too in the movement.
